title: One-to-one and onto
objectives: Prove that a function is one-to-one or onto, and build its inverse when it is both.

screens.title: Desks nobody sits on
screens.prose: The seating function from last lesson: $f(\text{Ana}) = \text{FX}$, $f(\text{Ben}) = \text{Rates}$, $f(\text{Cal}) = \text{FX}$.

state.caption: Traders in $A$ on the left, desks in $B$ on the right

screens.question: Tap every desk that no arrow reaches.

hints.text: Follow each arrow to its desk.
The arrows land on Rates and FX.
Equities and Credit have no arrow arriving.

feedback.correct: Right. Equities and Credit are never reached.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap the desks with no arrowhead on them.

byKey.one: You found Equities. Credit has no arrow either.
byKey.fx: Two arrows reach FX, from Ana and from Cal.

explain.text: The arrows land only on Rates and FX, the image of $f$. Equities and Credit are in the codomain but never hit. So $f$ does not reach every desk.

screens.title: A shared desk
screens.prose: A function that reaches every element of its codomain is **onto**. The seating $f$ misses two desks, so it is not onto. Now look at the traders.

state.caption: Traders in $A$ on the left, desks in $B$ on the right

screens.question: Tap the two traders who share a desk.

hints.text: Find a desk with two arrows arriving.
Two arrows reach FX.
Ana and Cal both sit on FX.

feedback.correct: Right. Ana and Cal share FX.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the desk two arrows reach, then tap where they start.

explain.text: $f(\text{Ana}) = f(\text{Cal}) = \text{FX}$, with $\text{Ana} \ne \text{Cal}$. Two different inputs give one output. That is allowed for a function, but it is a property worth naming.

screens.title: One-to-one
screens.prose: $f : A \to B$ is **one-to-one** when different inputs give different outputs. As a rule: $f(a_1) = f(a_2) \Rightarrow a_1 = a_2$. By its contrapositive from If, then, that is $a_1 \ne a_2 \Rightarrow f(a_1) \ne f(a_2)$.

state.caption: Traders in $A$ on the left, desks in $B$ on the right

screens.question: Which single change makes $f$ one-to-one?

options.text: Move Cal from FX to Equities
Move Ben from Rates to FX
options.why: You moved Ben onto FX as well. Now three traders share one desk.

options.text: Add a second arrow, Cal to Credit
options.why: You gave Cal two desks. Then $f$ is no longer a function.
You changed the codomain. Ana and Cal still share FX.

hints.text: The trouble is two arrows meeting at FX.
Send one of Ana and Cal somewhere empty.
Moving Cal to Equities leaves every desk with at most one arrow.

feedback.correct: Right. Now no desk has two arrows.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Separate the two traders who share FX.

byKey.drop: You shrank the codomain. That helps onto, not one-to-one: FX still has two arrows.

explain.text: One-to-one means no desk receives two arrows. Moving Cal to Equities gives FX, Rates and Equities one arrow each. Credit is still missed, so the new $f$ is one-to-one but not onto.

screens.title: How to start
screens.prose: Claim: $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $f(x) = 3x + 2$, is one-to-one. A table of values is a tempting start.
screens.question: Which opening starts a proof that $f$ is one-to-one?

options.why: You checked examples. Three rows cannot cover every pair of real numbers.
You proved equal inputs give equal outputs. That holds for every function; it is not one-to-one.
You proved the contrapositive of the function rule. It is true for any function, so it shows nothing here.

hints.text: Write the definition: $f(a_1) = f(a_2) \Rightarrow a_1 = a_2$.
A direct proof of an implication assumes its hypothesis.
Assume $f(a) = f(b)$ for arbitrary $a$, $b$, and aim for $a = b$.

feedback.correct: Right. Assume equal outputs and derive equal inputs.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the hypothesis of $f(a) = f(b) \Rightarrow a = b$.

byKey.examples: You chose to check rows of the table. Examples are evidence. The proof must take arbitrary $a$ and $b$.
byKey.func: You started from $a = b$. That direction is what makes $f$ a function, and every function passes it.

explain.text: One-to-one is $f(a) = f(b) \Rightarrow a = b$, so we assume $f(a) = f(b)$ for arbitrary $a$ and $b$. Checking rows proves nothing about the others. Starting from $a = b$ proves the wrong direction.

screens.title: The one-to-one proof
screens.prose: Now the proof itself, for $f(x) = 3x + 2$ on $\mathbb{R}$.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.why: You divided only part of each side by 3. Subtract 2 first, then divide both sides by 3.

hints.text: Start from the opening you chose.
Write out $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, then undo $+2$ and $\times 3$.

feedback.correct: Right. Assume, unpack, undo the $+2$, undo the $\times 3$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Unpack $f$, then undo its steps one at a time.

byKey.d1: You kept the line dividing only $3a$ and $3b$ by 3. Each side must be divided as a whole.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.
byKey.s1: The proof opens by assuming $f(a) = f(b)$.

explain.text: We assumed equal outputs and undid the rule step by step until the inputs matched. The steps work for any real $a$ and $b$. So $f$ is one-to-one.

screens.title: Reasons
screens.prose: Give the reason for each line after the first.
screens.question: Drop a reason into each slot. One reason is not used.

tokens.text: Divide both sides by 3, which is not 0

hints.text: Line 2 writes $f(a)$ out in full.
Line 3 removes the $+2$; line 4 removes the $\times 3$.
2: definition of $f$. 3: subtract 2. 4: divide by 3, safe because $3 \ne 0$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what changed from one line to the next.

byKey.sq: No line squares anything. Squaring would also lose information, since $(-a)^2 = a^2$.
byKey.div: Line 4 divides both sides by 3. That is safe because $3 \ne 0$.
byKey.def: Line 2 replaces $f(a)$ by $3a + 2$: the definition of $f$.

explain.text: Line 2 uses the definition of $f$. Lines 3 and 4 undo the $+2$ and the $\times 3$. Dividing by 3 is allowed only because $3 \ne 0$.

screens.title: Onto
screens.prose: $f$ is onto if every $y \in \mathbb{R}$ is hit: $\forall y\ \exists x,\ f(x) = y$. Let $y \in \mathbb{R}$. We need a witness $x$, as in For all and there exists.
screens.question: Which $x$ has $f(x) = y$? Write it in terms of $y$.

hints.text: Solve $3x + 2 = y$ for $x$.
Subtract 2 first, then divide by 3.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $3x + 2 = y$ for $x$, undoing the last step first.

byKey.order: You divided before subtracting. Undo the last step, $+2$, first.
byKey.fwd: You applied $f$ to $y$. We need the input that $f$ sends to $y$.

explain.text: Choose $x = \dfrac{y - 2}{3}$, a real number for every real $y$. Then $f(x) = 3 \cdot \dfrac{y - 2}{3} + 2 = y$. Every $y$ has a witness, so $f$ is onto.

screens.title: A bijection and its inverse
screens.prose:
A function that is one-to-one and onto is a **bijection**. Each $y$ then comes from exactly one $x$, so we can run $f$ backwards. Only a bijection has an inverse:

$$f^{-1}(y) = \frac{y - 2}{3}$$
screens.question: What is $f^{-1}(11)$?

byKey.fwd: You worked out $f(11) = 35$. The inverse runs the other way.
byKey.sign: You added 2 instead of subtracting it: $\dfrac{11 + 2}{3}$.

screens.title: Squaring
screens.prose: $g(x) = x^2$. The rule is fixed, but the domain and codomain are ours to choose. $[0, \infty)$ is the set of reals $x \ge 0$.
screens.question: Which are true? Select all that apply.

options.why: You shrank the codomain only. $g(-2) = g(2) = 4$ still, so it is not one-to-one.
You missed the negative outputs. No real $x$ has $x^2 = -1$.

hints.text: Test one-to-one with $-2$ and $2$. Test onto with $-1$.
The dashed line $y = -1$ never meets the curve.
On $\mathbb{R}$, $g(-2) = g(2)$ and $-1$ is missed. On $[0, \infty)$ each $y \ge 0$ has exactly one $x = \sqrt{y}$.

feedback.correct: Right. Whether $x^2$ is one-to-one or onto depends on the domain and codomain.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each claim with $-2$, $2$ and $-1$.

byKey.half: You fixed onto but not one-to-one. To fix one-to-one, restrict the domain.
byKey.onto: You claimed onto over $\mathbb{R}$. The line $y = -1$ misses the curve.

explain.text: On $\mathbb{R}$, $g(-2) = g(2) = 4$ and nothing maps to $-1$, so $g$ is neither. Restricting both sets to $[0, \infty)$ leaves one $x = \sqrt{y}$ for each $y$. As in Functions, restricting $x^2$ gives it an inverse.

screens.title: Counting one-to-one functions
screens.prose: Seat Ana, Ben and Cal on the four desks with no desk shared. The grid shows one way, with the cells ruled out greyed.

state.caption: Ana takes FX, so Ben cannot. Cal cannot take FX or Rates.

screens.question: How many one-to-one functions are there from the 3 traders to the 4 desks?

hints.text: Ana has 4 choices. How many are left for Ben?
Ben has 3 desks left, then Cal has 2.
$4 \times 3 \times 2 = 24$.

feedback.correct: Right. $4 \times 3 \times 2 = 24$, and none of them is onto.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each trader has one fewer desk than the one before.

byKey.all: You allowed sharing: $4^3 = 64$ counts every function.
byKey.perm3: You used $3!$, as if there were 3 desks. There are 4.

explain.text: Ana has 4 choices, Ben 3 and Cal 2, so there are 24 one-to-one functions. None is onto: three arrows cannot reach four desks. With 3 traders and 3 desks, one-to-one forces onto, and there are $3! = 6$ bijections.

screens.title: Ids, hashes and currencies
screens.prose: Three maps from a trading system. A hash sends each of 5,000 order ids to one of 1,024 buckets. A converter turns £ into \$ at a fixed 1.25.
screens.question: Which are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Trade to id must be one-to-one: two trades with one id is a booking error
£ to \$ at 1.25 is a bijection; its inverse divides by 1.25
A good enough hash makes order id to bucket one-to-one
options.why: You trusted the hash. With 5,000 ids and 1,024 buckets, some bucket must get two ids.

options.text: Trade to id must be onto: every possible id must be used
options.why: Unused ids are fine. Only sharing an id breaks the booking.

hints.text: For each map, ask: can two inputs share an output?
There are more order ids than buckets.
Ids must be one-to-one. The hash cannot be. The converter is undone by dividing by 1.25.

feedback.correct: Right. Ids must be one-to-one, the hash cannot be, and conversion is a bijection.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the sizes of domain and codomain, and ask what each map must do.

byKey.hash: You allowed a one-to-one hash. More inputs than outputs force a shared bucket.
byKey.onto: You asked every id to be used. A booking system needs distinct ids, not all of them.

explain.text: If 5,000 ids go into 1,024 buckets, two ids must share a bucket: the pigeonhole idea. Trade ids must be one-to-one, or a booking is ambiguous. £200 becomes \$250, and \$250 divided by 1.25 is £200 again.

ideas: One-to-one: $f(a_1) = f(a_2) \Rightarrow a_1 = a_2$. Prove it by assuming $f(a) = f(b)$ and deriving $a = b$.
Onto: $\forall y \in B\ \exists x \in A,\ f(x) = y$. Prove it by fixing $y$ and naming a witness $x$.
A bijection is both, and only a bijection has an inverse. Whether $x^2$ is one, the other or both depends on its domain and codomain.
summary.trap: Checking examples, or showing equal inputs give equal outputs, does not prove one-to-one.

byKey.fwd: You worked out $f(-4) = -10$. The inverse runs the other way.

quiz.prose: Three analysts are each given one of three different reports to check, with no report checked twice.
quiz.question: How many such one-to-one functions are there?

feedback.correct: Right. $3! = 6$, and each one is onto too.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The first analyst has 3 choices, the next 2, the last 1.

byKey.all: You allowed sharing: $3^3 = 27$ counts every function.

explain.text: There are $3 \times 2 \times 1 = 6$ one-to-one functions. Three different outputs from three inputs use every report, so each is onto: a bijection.

quiz.prose: We want to prove $h : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $h(x) = 5x - 1$, is onto.
quiz.question: Which is a correct first two lines?

options.why: That opens a proof of one-to-one, not onto.
You checked two outputs. Onto needs every $y$.

options.text: Let $x \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $h(x) = 5x - 1$ is a real number.
options.why: You started from $x$. That shows $h$ lands in $\mathbb{R}$, not that every $y$ is hit.

feedback.correct: Right. Start from an arbitrary $y$ and name its witness.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Onto is $\forall y\ \exists x$: start with $y$.

explain.text: Onto is $\forall y\ \exists x,\ h(x) = y$. So we fix any $y$ and give a witness $x = \dfrac{y + 1}{5}$. Then $h(x) = (y + 1) - 1 = y$.

quiz.prose: A converter sends £ to \$ at a fixed rate: $c(p) = 1.25p$.
quiz.question: A client holds \$250. How many pounds is that, using $c^{-1}$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The inverse divides by 1.25.

byKey.fwd: You multiplied by 1.25 again. $c^{-1}$ divides by 1.25.
